series.title: B.L.E.S.S.
series.description: A 5-week series exploring five missional practices so that we can join in on what God is doing in the lives of those around us.
series.bigIdea: God uses the unlikely to accomplish the impossible, and He invites us to join in.
series.leaderGuide:
B.L.E.S.S. is a 5-week series exploring how God uses the unlikely to accomplish the impossible. Rather than letting culture dictate their future, students will be equipped with an evangelism toolkit of five simple, everyday missional practices: Begin with prayer, Listen with care, Eat together, Serve with love, and Share the story.

By walking through these habits alongside powerful biblical narratives, students will move past a "one-time wish list" mindset and actively join in on what God is doing in the lives of those around them.

Two tools return every week. S.T.A.R.S. helps students dig into Scripture: Something familiar, Themes, Attributes of God, Repetition, Something surprising. FRANCS helps them name the people God has placed around them: Friends, Relatives, Acquaintances, Neighbors, Classmates, Strangers.

services.title: Begin With Prayer
services.bigIdea: Before we try to reach people, we pray for them.
services.objectives:
Understand that prayer is a habit, not a one-time wish list
See that prayer is about growth, not gifts
Map the people in their world using FRANCS and choose who to pray for

parts.title: Introduction
parts.script: Today we will be talking about the power of praying for our friends, family, and community members who do not yet know Jesus.

parts.title: Illustration: Dead Battery

supplies.name: Phone, or a slide of a dead-battery icon

parts.instructions: Show an image of a dead battery icon on screen, or hold up your own phone. Have a personal story ready.
parts.script:
What would be the worst time for your phone to die? Have you ever had your phone die at an awkward time?

[Allow time for answers, then share your story.]

I have seen people shamelessly ask strangers to borrow a charger. When a phone dies, people get irritable. The same is true for us and prayer. We try to share God's love or shine a light without connecting to the true power source!

parts.title: Transition
parts.script:
"Begin with Prayer" is the first missional practice in our BLESS evangelism toolkit.

Before we dig into prayer and today's passage, let's pause to ask the Holy Spirit to shine light on the text, be our teacher, and transform us.

[Pray.]

parts.title: Read: Colossians 1:3–12
parts.script: "We always thank God, the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, when we pray for you, because we have heard of your faith… the gospel is bearing fruit and growing throughout the whole world… You learned it from Epaphras, our dear fellow servant, who is a faithful minister of Christ… For this reason, since the day we heard about you, we have not stopped praying for you. We continually ask God to fill you with the knowledge of his will… bearing fruit in every good work, growing in the knowledge of God…"

parts.title: Theological Insight
parts.script:
Paul's letter to the Colossians exists in our Bible today because one person who was not an apostle went home and told friends about Jesus.

Epaphras (Colossians 1:7, 4:12) was one of the first to bless others with the gospel. He was "always wrestling in prayer" for his friends and neighbors.

Paul wrote this letter to strengthen the faith of the Colossians and help them work together to share Jesus.

parts.title: S.T.A.R.S. Method
parts.instructions: Read the passage again and explore it together using the S.T.A.R.S. method. Let students call out what they notice for each letter.
parts.script:
1. Something familiar: What have you heard about before? (fruit, the fruit of the Spirit, endurance)
2. Themes: What theme sticks out? (prayer, and praying for specific things like the knowledge of God)
3. Attributes of God: What does this passage say about God? (His glorious power; He enables us)
4. Repetition: What occurs more than once? (look for words like "all," "every," or "continually")
5. Something surprising: What was unexpected? What stood out to you right away?

parts.title: Point 1: Prayer is a habit, not a one-time wish list
parts.script:
[Repetition] "Always… when we pray" (v. 3), "not stopped praying" (v. 9), and "continually ask" (v. 9).

Prayer isn't a one-time wish list. It is a constant conversation with God as we seek for our family, friends, and neighbors to know Jesus. Epaphras didn't just pray once in a while. He built a habit of ongoing prayer.

parts.title: Point 2: Prayer is about growth, not gifts
parts.script:
[Repetition] The gospel is "bearing fruit and growing" (v. 6), and the people are "bearing fruit in every good work" (v. 10).

The gospel is alive and brings growth! Like the Sea of Galilee, it is meant to produce life. When we connect to God, we can expect to see new growth in our lives and in those we pray for.

parts.title: Point 3: Prayer is for "all" and "every," not just some
parts.script:
[Repetition] "Love… for all God's people" (v. 4), "all the wisdom" (v. 9), "please him in every way" (v. 10), and "strengthened with all power" (v. 11).

God doesn't want just a piece of our lives. God wants to bless every part of us so we can bless everyone around us. God can use anyone, from anywhere, to bless everyone.

parts.title: Mapping Your Influence (FRANCS)
parts.instructions:
The FRANCS model is a tool to help students think about, pray for, and bless the people around them. Have everyone write down names in each category:

• Friends: Who do you choose to spend time with regularly?
• Relatives: Who is in your immediate and extended family?
• Acquaintances: Who do you cross paths with regularly?
• Neighbors: Who can you pray for in your neighborhood?
• Classmates: Who do you see regularly in class, the lunchroom, or the bus?
• Strangers: Who do you pass by often but have never really met?

parts.title: This Week: Next Steps
parts.script:
Circle names: Take a moment to pray, then circle the names you sense God inviting you to focus on.

Make a plan: Set a reminder on your phone or planner to pray for them every day.

Find a partner: Share your plan with someone who can check in on you and cheer you on.

services.title: Listen With Care
services.bigIdea: We notice where God is working and join Him in pointing others to Jesus.
services.objectives:
Listen to the Holy Spirit and follow His nudges
Listen with care to the people around them
Make reading God's word a regular rhythm

parts.title: Introduction
parts.script: Today we are exploring the second missional practice of BLESS. Can anyone remind us what each letter in BLESS stands for and what we learned last week?

parts.title: Illustration: Back-to-Back Drawing
parts.instructions:
The setup: Pair students up and have them sit back-to-back. Give Student A a blank piece of paper and a pen. Give Student B a card with a complex, abstract geometric shape on it. You might also use an object like a house with a chimney and a specific tree.

The activity: Student B describes the shape without naming it so Student A can draw it. Student A is not allowed to speak; they can only listen. Student B has 60 seconds.

Compare the drawings to the original cards. This should be funny.

parts.title: Transition
parts.script: Listening isn't just about hearing words; it's about a two-way connection. Without listening with care or asking thoughtful questions, we usually end up with a mess.

parts.title: Theological Insight
parts.script: The Book of Acts was written by Luke, who also wrote the Gospel of Luke. Luke's Gospel is about the life, teachings, and works of Jesus, and Acts is about the work of the Holy Spirit, which led to the growth of the early church.

parts.title: Read: Acts 8:26–38
parts.script:
Now an angel of the Lord said to Philip, "Go south to the road—the desert road—that goes down from Jerusalem to Gaza." So he started out, and on his way he met an Ethiopian eunuch, an important official in charge of all the treasury of the Kandake (which means "queen of the Ethiopians"). This man had gone to Jerusalem to worship, and on his way home was sitting in his chariot reading the Book of Isaiah the prophet. The Spirit told Philip, "Go to that chariot and stay near it."

Then Philip ran up to the chariot and heard the man reading Isaiah the prophet. "Do you understand what you are reading?" Philip asked.

"How can I," he said, "unless someone explains it to me?" So he invited Philip to come up and sit with him.

This is the passage of Scripture the eunuch was reading: "He was led like a sheep to the slaughter, and as a lamb before its shearer is silent, so he did not open his mouth. In his humiliation he was deprived of justice. Who can speak of his descendants? For his life was taken from the earth."

The eunuch asked Philip, "Tell me, please, who is the prophet talking about, himself or someone else?" Then Philip began with that very passage of Scripture and told him the good news about Jesus. As they traveled along the road, they came to some water and the eunuch said, "Look, here is water. What can stand in the way of my being baptized?" And he gave orders to stop the chariot. Then both Philip and the eunuch went down into the water and Philip baptized him.

parts.title: S.T.A.R.S. Method
parts.instructions: Read the passage again and explore it together using the S.T.A.R.S. method. Let students call out what they notice for each letter.
parts.script:
1. Something familiar: What have you heard about before?
2. Themes: What theme sticks out?
3. Attributes of God: What does this passage say about God?
4. Repetition: What occurs more than once?
5. Something surprising: What was unexpected? What stood out to you right away?

parts.title: Point 1: Philip listened to the Holy Spirit
parts.script:
[Themes: God speaking to His followers] "Now an angel of the Lord said to Philip" (v. 26).

In verses 26 and 29, Philip receives two specific prompts. First, an angel tells him to go to a "desert road." Later the Spirit tells him, "Go to that chariot and stay near it." Philip doesn't ask questions; he simply obeys the next immediate nudge.

We often miss opportunities because we are too busy or we are not listening for the Holy Spirit. Let's practice spiritual alertness this week. At the beginning of each day, ask God to give you spiritual ears and a sensitive heart to hear from the Holy Spirit. Or, before you eat each meal, ask God to open your ears to hear the voice of the Holy Spirit.

parts.title: Point 2: Philip listened to the Ethiopian man
parts.script:
[Something surprising: reading Scripture] "Then Philip ran up to the chariot and heard the man reading Isaiah" (v. 30).

Being a witness for the gospel of Jesus Christ requires learning to listen with care. When we listen with care, we are listening for specific needs, questions, and the context of the person we are with.

When talking with your FRANCS, practice listening more than you speak. Ask more questions than you give answers. Listen for their spiritual thirsts, their fears, their hopes, or their confusion before offering a solution.

parts.title: Point 3: Philip listened to God's word
parts.script:
[Something familiar: Scripture pointing to Jesus] "Then Philip began with that very passage of Scripture and told him the good news about Jesus" (v. 35).

We cannot share what we do not know. Practice making it a habit or regular rhythm to read the Bible, to listen to God, and to be transformed by the grace and truth of the gospel as you read. God not only speaks in the word, He also speaks through the word.

parts.title: Weekly Challenge: Listening Exercises
parts.script:
Using the FRANCS model we learned last week, prepare to listen well. Throughout the week, listen to others using the guide below and come prepared to share what you heard next week.

Someone says they are tired. Are they physically tired, spiritually fatigued, or emotionally overwhelmed?

Someone mentions a hobby or interest. Listen for what makes them happy.

Someone says, "I don't know." Are they revealing a need for wisdom or guidance?

Someone talks about a problem with someone. Does that reveal a need for peace?

Someone celebrates something small. Listen for a chance to encourage them.

You sense a nudge from God. It could be a random idea to sit by someone, to say hi to someone you don't know well, or something else.

parts.title: Discussion
parts.script:
1. Who is the best listener you know? What do they do that makes you feel heard and understood? What are some pro tips they might give for listening?
2. Of the three things Philip listened to (the Holy Spirit, the other person, God's word), which do you think you are best at listening to? Where do you need the most practice?
3. How was God already at work in the story of Philip and the Ethiopian man?

parts.title: Closing Prayer
parts.script: Pray that God would give each person spiritual ears this week: to hear the Holy Spirit, to listen with care to their FRANCS, and to hear God through His word.

services.title: Eat Together
services.bigIdea: Sharing a meal is one of the most powerful ways to show someone they belong, and Jesus used it on purpose.
services.objectives:
See how powerful an invitation can be
Be willing to get close to the need
Practice being present with the people around them

parts.title: Introduction
parts.script: Today we're exploring the third missional practice of BLESS. Can someone remind us what each letter in BLESS stands for and what we learned last week?

parts.title: Illustration: The Ps and Qs
parts.instructions:
The goal: Find common ground through rapid-fire menu choices. No supplies needed.

The activity: Invite students to stand in the center of the room. Designate one side of the room as Option A and the other as Option B. Call out a food pairing and have students move to the side they prefer. Once they land, they have 30 seconds to find someone on their side, preferably someone they don't know well, and answer the follow-up question.

1. Tacos or Pizza? What's your favorite food from childhood?
2. Savory or Sweet? What's your favorite snack and drink combo for a movie night?
3. Homemade or Fast Food? If you had to cook a four-star meal yourself, what would you make?
4. Soup or Salad? What's a food other people like but you do not?
5. Pancakes or Omelet? What are your favorite ingredients for your pancake or omelet?
6. "Table for two" or "Party of 8"? If you could invite anyone alive today to share a meal, who would you choose?
7. Hot Cocoa or Coffee? What is the most memorable or meaningful meal you've ever had?

The lesson: Food can set the table for connection and conversations with anyone.

parts.title: Transition
parts.script: Why do you think God made food with such a wide range of enjoyable flavors, and our mouths with such enhanced taste buds? What does this say about our Creator?

parts.title: Theological Insight
parts.script: Today we will learn about eating together from Jesus in Luke 5:27–32. It is the story of Jesus and Levi, a tax collector. Tax collectors were despised by the people of Israel because they were notorious for their greed, robbery, and exploitation of others. They were among the last people God-fearing people would want in their homes or at their tables.

parts.title: Read: Luke 5:27–32
parts.script:
27 After this, Jesus went out and saw a tax collector by the name of Levi sitting at his tax booth. "Follow me," Jesus said to him, 28 and Levi got up, left everything and followed him.

29 Then Levi held a great banquet for Jesus at his house, and a large crowd of tax collectors and others were eating with them. 30 But the Pharisees and the teachers of the law who belonged to their sect complained to his disciples, "Why do you eat and drink with tax collectors and sinners?"

31 Jesus answered them, "It is not the healthy who need a doctor, but the sick. 32 I have not come to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance."

parts.title: S.T.A.R.S. Method
parts.instructions: Read the passage again and explore it together using the S.T.A.R.S. method. Let students call out what they notice for each letter.
parts.script:
1. Something familiar: What have you heard about before?
2. Themes: What theme sticks out?
3. Attributes of God: What does this passage say about God?
4. Repetition: What occurs more than once?
5. Something surprising: What was unexpected? What stood out to you right away?

parts.title: Point 1: Invitations are powerful
parts.script:
[Everyone wants to be included and invited.]

Verses 27–28 say that at Jesus's invitation, Levi got up from his tax table, left everything (money, power, security, and favor), and followed Jesus.

Studies show that 70–80 percent of young people today (Gen Z) report struggling with loneliness. Though teens today are digital natives and well connected online, they crave relationships IRL (in real life). More than 50 percent are looking for someone to talk with about their interests and passions. That means you're not alone. Half of your peers would be happy to be invited to hang out, share a meal, and talk about faith in person.

parts.title: Point 2: Get close to the need
parts.script:
[Key point: We must be willing to get close to the need if we want to faithfully meet the need.]

Jesus drew close to people who didn't have life figured out, and to those who thought they did! They all needed Jesus to draw near and share the truth of the gospel with them.

As we seek to bless people, we get close and share life with them. We do not need to be afraid to engage people who are imperfect or judgmental. As we follow the Holy Spirit in moving closer to people, we show them that we see them as God sees them and that we care about them. When we become proximate to people, eat a meal with them, listen with care, and pray for them, we develop eyes to see the transforming work God is doing in their life.

parts.title: Point 3: Presence is vital
parts.script:
[Eating together is like a cheat code for friendship.]

Levi didn't just invite Jesus to grab a quick snack. He threw a huge party with a large crowd. Jesus didn't just preach and run. He stayed, sat, hung out. He met Levi's friends and became friends with them too.

Life moves fast. Between classes, practice, clubs, and scrolling on your phone, we rarely give people our full attention. But when we sit down to eat with someone and get to know them, the walls can come down. We can stop worrying so much about how we look or whether others in the room will approve of who we are eating with. We start connecting and building community.

parts.title: Discussion
parts.script:
1. If you could host a table for four with you, Jesus, and two other people, who would you invite? Why would you choose them?
2. In today's passage, the religious leaders were shocked that Jesus ate with "sinners and tax collectors." If Jesus were walking through your school cafeteria today, which table or group of people do you think it would be surprising for him to sit with? Why?
3. Levi left everything—his job, money, and security—when Jesus invited him to become his disciple. Why do you think an invitation to follow or be included is so powerful for someone who feels lonely or like an outsider?
4. Think about your FRANCS. Who is someone you see often but haven't actually drawn close to yet? What is one small way you could move closer to them this week?
5. Why do you think eating together makes it easier to have real conversations? How does the vibe of a conversation change when there is food on the table versus standing in a hallway between classes?
6. Presence is powerful. What is one way you can show a friend that they are more important than your phone the next time you hang out?
7. Jesus said he came for the sick. That means our lives don't have to be perfect or put together to be at his table. How does knowing that Jesus wants to eat with messy people who make mistakes change the way you view him and others?

parts.title: Closing Prayer
parts.script: Pray for courage to invite someone to share a meal this week, and for eyes to see the people who are waiting to be included.

services.title: Serve With Love
services.bigIdea: Serving with love means being a real friend instead of treating them like something to fix.
services.objectives:
See that God equally values every person (upside-down value)
Understand that Jesus centers His kingdom on people the world overlooks (inside-out vision)
Choose solidarity over charity and justice over good deeds (right-side-up venture)

parts.title: Introduction
parts.script:
Today we're exploring the fourth missional practice of BLESS. Can someone remind us what each letter in BLESS stands for and what we learned last week?

Would anyone be willing to share a story about how God showed up as you shared a meal or snack with someone this past week?

parts.title: Illustration: The Hidden Message

supplies.name: Paper slip (2.5" × 0.75") with "winner" written in pencil

parts.instructions:
The setup: Write the word "winner" on a slip of paper measuring 2.5" × 0.75" and place it face-down at the bottom of a box of standard playing cards. Prepare enough boxes for groups of 4–8 to each have one.

Give a prepared box of playing cards to each group of students.
parts.script:
There is a hidden message in each of these boxes of 52 standard playing cards. When I say go, your job is to open the box, take out the cards, and be the first group or person to find the message and read it out loud. The first person to find and read the secret message will win a prize. You'll have 52 seconds to find the message. Are you ready?… Set… GO!

[Debrief] What was frustrating about this game? Why? How did you feel when you realized your cards didn't have any special message? How do you think this activity mirrors real life? What life lessons could we learn from this activity?

parts.title: Read: Matthew 25:31–46
parts.script:
31 "When the Son of Man comes in his glory, and all the angels with him, he will sit on his glorious throne. 32 All the nations will be gathered before him, and he will separate the people one from another as a shepherd separates the sheep from the goats. 33 He will put the sheep on his right and the goats on his left.

34 "Then the King will say to those on his right, 'Come, you who are blessed by my Father; take your inheritance, the kingdom prepared for you since the creation of the world. 35 For I was hungry and you gave me something to eat, I was thirsty and you gave me something to drink, I was a stranger and you invited me in, 36 I needed clothes and you clothed me, I was sick and you looked after me, I was in prison and you came to visit me.'

37 "Then the righteous will answer him, 'Lord, when did we see you hungry and feed you, or thirsty and give you something to drink? 38 When did we see you a stranger and invite you in, or needing clothes and clothe you? 39 When did we see you sick or in prison and go to visit you?'

40 "The King will reply, 'Truly I tell you, whatever you did for one of the least of these brothers and sisters of mine, you did for me.'

41 "Then he will say to those on his left, 'Depart from me, you who are cursed, into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels. 42 For I was hungry and you gave me nothing to eat, I was thirsty and you gave me nothing to drink, 43 I was a stranger and you did not invite me in, I needed clothes and you did not clothe me, I was sick and in prison and you did not look after me.'

44 "They also will answer, 'Lord, when did we see you hungry or thirsty or a stranger or needing clothes or sick or in prison, and did not help you?'

45 "He will reply, 'Truly I tell you, whatever you did not do for one of the least of these, you did not do for me.'

46 "Then they will go away to eternal punishment, but the righteous to eternal life."

parts.title: S.T.A.R.S. Method
parts.instructions: Read the passage again and explore it together using the S.T.A.R.S. method. Let students call out what they notice for each letter.
parts.script:
1. Something familiar: What have you heard about before?
2. Themes: What theme sticks out?
3. Attributes of God: What does this passage say about God?
4. Repetition: What occurs more than once?
5. Something surprising: What was unexpected? What stood out to you right away?

parts.title: Reflection Questions
parts.script:
1. What do you hear God saying to you through this passage?
2. What was surprising about this story?
3. What feelings or emotions stirred in you in response to this passage?

parts.title: Point 1: Upside-Down Value
parts.script:
In our opening game, you all scrambled for the cards. Why? Because that's where we assumed the value was. In life we tend to do the same thing. We tend to place value on people with power, influencers, and people who can do something for us.

This parable helps us see that God equally values all people, no matter their circumstance. That includes people society typically overlooks. Serving with love means seeing the value in every person and affirming that every person is equally created in God's image and loved by God.

parts.title: Point 2: Inside-Out Vision
parts.script:
Jesus centers his kingdom on people the world marginalizes. He moves the outsiders to the inside and stands with them in solidarity. In fact, in this passage insiders and outsiders in the kingdom of God are defined by how they see, listen with care, and respond to the needs of "the least of these."

In verse 45 we read Jesus's reply: "Truly I tell you, whatever you did not do for one of the least of these, you did not do for me." Jesus is saying that this type of love is one of the things that distinguishes his disciples in the world.

parts.title: Point 3: Right-Side-Up Venture: Building the Kingdom
parts.script:
In a way, serving with love is to "right-side-up" the world so that it looks the way God desires. That requires us to go beyond charity, good deeds, and good will.

[Solidarity over charity] Charity is top-down and often just gives money from a distance. Solidarity is a side-by-side friendship. It means putting others first, listening to their needs, and standing up for people who are mistreated or ignored.

[Justice over good deeds] True love doesn't ignore suffering. While good deeds give out food, biblical justice asks why people are hungry in the first place. It works to change broken systems so everyone has a seat at the table.

[Upside-down vision] In God's kingdom, the last are first. When we focus on welcoming the poor, the stranger, and the outsider, we show that God's love is for everyone and that every single person has dignity.

parts.title: Weekly Challenge: Beyond the Project
parts.script:
This week our challenge is to assess our vision and values.

Step 1: Identify the invisible. Think of your school hallway, bus, neighborhood, sports team, or club. Who is a person that others tend to overlook? [Action] Write their name or a description of them on a note.

Step 2: Move from "for" to "with." Don't just do something for them. Find a way to be with them. [Action] This week, begin with prayer, listen with care, and eat together. Be attentive to the ways the Holy Spirit prompts you to serve this person with love. How might you remind them that they are equally loved and made in God's image? How might you stand with them in solidarity?

parts.title: Discussion
parts.script:
1. Top-down vs. side-by-side: Have you ever had someone help you but make you feel small or judged? How is that different from a real friend who just stands by you?
2. The "why" of justice: Instead of just doing a quick good deed, how does it change things when we stop and ask why someone is struggling in the first place?
3. Applying the vision: If our youth group put the "last first," who would be the VIPs at our next meeting? What would we need to change to make that happen?
4. Inside-out value: What is one choice you can make this week to sacrifice your own comfort or "popularity" to help someone else (like sitting with someone who is lonely)?
5. The goal of solidarity: Serving with love isn't just a one-time project. How do the BLESS habits help us build real, long-term friendships with people?

parts.title: Closing Prayer
parts.script: Pray for the person each student wrote down, and ask God for eyes to see people the way He sees them.

services.title: Share the Story
services.bigIdea: Your story matters because it connects your life experiences directly to God's story.
services.objectives:
Learn the five-finger Story Tool for sharing their faith
Connect their own story to God's story
Invite a friend to take one small next step toward Jesus

parts.title: Introduction
parts.leaderNotes: This lesson is longer than the others because it includes a deeper dive into the gospel and time to practice using the Story Tool. Consider extending your gathering time or splitting the content over two weeks.
parts.script:
Today we are exploring the final missional practice of BLESS. Can someone remind everyone what each letter in BLESS stands for and what we have learned so far?

Would anyone be willing to share a story of how God showed up as you served someone with love this past week?

parts.title: Illustration: One-Sentence Story
parts.instructions:
The setup: Form circles of around 8–12 students. No supplies needed.

The activity: The leader begins a story with one sentence (for example, "There once was a student who found a strange envelope in the bottom of his locker"). Each person adds exactly one sentence to move the story forward.

The goal: Listen to the person before you so the story makes sense and reaches a resolution by the time it gets to the last person. Play a handful of rounds, then debrief.

• What was fun about this game? What was difficult about it?
• What lessons about life can we learn from this game?
• How do you think this game connects with our final letter in BLESS?

parts.title: Transition
parts.script:
In the game we all had to listen to the person before us to make sure our sentence connected to what they said, or the story wouldn't make sense. Our own lives are like that!

We are all part of a larger story—God's story—and we get to figure out how our life fits in with God's great narrative of love and redemption. Your story matters. Each person's story is a big deal. You may not feel like you have an amazing story, but your story points to one story that is—God's story.

parts.title: Read: John 4:1–26, 39–42
parts.script:
Now Jesus learned that the Pharisees had heard that he was gaining and baptizing more disciples than John— 2 although in fact it was not Jesus who baptized, but his disciples. 3 So he left Judea and went back once more to Galilee.

4 Now he had to go through Samaria. 5 So he came to a town in Samaria called Sychar, near the plot of ground Jacob had given to his son Joseph. 6 Jacob's well was there, and Jesus, tired as he was from the journey, sat down by the well. It was about noon.

7 When a Samaritan woman came to draw water, Jesus said to her, "Will you give me a drink?" 8 (His disciples had gone into the town to buy food.)

9 The Samaritan woman said to him, "You are a Jew and I am a Samaritan woman. How can you ask me for a drink?" (For Jews do not associate with Samaritans.)

10 Jesus answered her, "If you knew the gift of God and who it is that asks you for a drink, you would have asked him and he would have given you living water."

11 "Sir," the woman said, "you have nothing to draw with and the well is deep. Where can you get this living water? 12 Are you greater than our father Jacob, who gave us the well and drank from it himself, as did also his sons and his livestock?"

[Continue reading through verse 26.]

25 The woman said, "I know that Messiah" (called Christ) "is coming. When he comes, he will explain everything to us." 26 Then Jesus declared, "I, the one speaking to you—I am he."

39 Many of the Samaritans from that town believed in him because of the woman's testimony, "He told me everything I ever did." 40 So when the Samaritans came to him, they urged him to stay with them, and he stayed two days. 41 And because of his words many more became believers.

42 They said to the woman, "We no longer believe just because of what you said; now we have heard for ourselves, and we know that this man really is the Savior of the world."

parts.title: S.T.A.R.S. Method
parts.instructions: Read the passage again and explore it together using the S.T.A.R.S. method. Let students call out what they notice for each letter.
parts.script:
1. Something familiar: What have you heard about before?
2. Themes: What theme sticks out?
3. Attributes of God: What does this passage say about God?
4. Repetition: What occurs more than once?
5. Something surprising: What was unexpected? What stood out to you right away?

parts.title: The Story Tool
parts.script: The Story Tool is easy to remember because you can use your hand to illustrate it. It has five parts, one for each digit.
parts.leaderNotes: Feel free to choose a strategy or tool for sharing the gospel that best suits you and your context. The original lesson points to an appendix with more in-depth resources.

parts.title: Point 1: Give their story a "thumbs up" (Affirm)
parts.script:
It starts by listening to your friend. (Remember, that's the "L" in BLESS.) What's going on in their life? Try to find things you have in common. Often this means connecting over tough times, feeling lost, or dealing with struggles.

Pay attention to how they feel, not just what they say. Try to put yourself in their shoes and imagine what they're going through. This is called empathy—feeling with them and understanding their experiences.

Affirming someone's story might sound like this:

• Echo back their story: "Wow, that's a lot of pressure."

• Recognize their emotion: "You must feel so anxious."

• Communicate care: "I'm sorry you're going through that right now."

parts.title: Point 2: Point to your story (Connect)
parts.script:
How can you show your friend you understand? Jesus understands our struggles because he experienced hard things too. He was treated unfairly, bullied, tempted, and he felt weak. He experienced our difficulties, and because of that, we can trust him.

When you share your story, be honest about your own struggles. This helps your friend know they are not alone. But don't make the story all about you. This part is just a bridge. The goal is to keep it short and connect your story to Jesus's story, showing how he made the real difference.

Pointing to your story might sound like this:

• Connect your experience: "I've been in a really stressful season before too."

• Confess your own struggle: "I often feel my own anxiety."

• Create a transition: "And I've only found one thing to help my anxiety."

[This is the setup that gets you to God's good news about Jesus. You won't share your whole story here, just enough to set up God's story.]

parts.title: Point 3: Lift up God's story (Exalt)
parts.script:
Jesus changes everything. The gospel is the story of how Jesus lived, died, and rose again to give us hope, forgiveness, and a fresh start. Sharing God's story doesn't mean sharing the whole Bible—just share the part that connects directly to what your friend is going through.

Use a simple statement + conclusion format:

• Grace: God loves us exactly as we are. So we don't have to perform or be perfect to experience His peace.

• Comfort: Jesus came to earth and felt the exact same stress and pain we do. So we can turn to Him whenever life feels heavy.

• Hope: Jesus died on the cross and beat death by rising again. So we don't have to worry, because His victory gives us daily strength.

parts.title: Point 4: Share your "changed" story (Reveal)
parts.script:
How did Jesus change you? When we start a relationship with Jesus, we get a new beginning and a new future. This part of your story is about the "before" and "after"—the difference Jesus made in your life.

• Grace: When I learned God loves me as I am, I let go of needing to be perfect. Now I have way more peace.

• Comfort: When I discovered Jesus understands my pain, I started talking to Him. Now I don't feel so overwhelmed.

• Hope: When I realized Jesus beat darkness and death, I stopped feeling helpless. Now I feel strong enough to face my fears.

parts.title: Point 5: Focus on their story (Suggest)
parts.script:
Help your friend take a small, comfortable next step to get to know Jesus. Don't push for a giant leap—just suggest one relevant idea and offer to do it with them.

• Talk to God like a friend.

• Read a chapter in a Gospel (like Mark or John).

• Download a Bible app for the verse of the day.

• Listen to an encouraging Christian song or playlist.

• Come to youth group or church with you.

• Practice gratitude or do a random act of kindness.

parts.title: Discussion
parts.script:
1. What stood out to you about how Jesus spoke to the Samaritan woman?
2. The Samaritan woman asks Jesus a lot of questions in this passage. What can we learn from her question-asking? How can we apply that in our conversations with our FRANCS?
3. What questions do your friends have about God, faith, religion, the Christian church, and spiritual things?
4. How would you respond if someone asked you, "Who is Jesus?"
5. The Samaritan woman couldn't keep the story of Jesus to herself. She told the whole town about him. Why do you think she did this?
6. Since many of us, like the Samaritan woman, have decided to follow Jesus, what are some things that hold us back from telling our community about the goodness of God the way she does?
7. John says, "Many of the Samaritans from that town believed in him because of the woman's testimony" (v. 39). If someone asked you about your testimony, or your Jesus story, what would you tell them? How would you tell your transformation story (the ring finger) in just a few sentences?
8. What's one small step you can invite a friend to take? How could you join them as they take this step?

parts.title: Closing Prayer
parts.script: Pray for the friends on each student's FRANCS list by name, and for the courage to share their story when the moment comes.
